Text: What red flag did you have right before a job offer that you wish you had heeded? Hindsight, as they say, is always 20/20. There’s a wisdom that only arrives with the benefit of looking back, a clarity that often comes too late. If I could rewind the clock and offer my younger self some sage advice, it would be to pay closer attention to the subtle warning signs I brushed aside before accepting a job offer at a particularly toxic company. Looking back, the first red flag, which I foolishly ignored, was the sheer speed of the hiring process. I was interviewed, offered the position, and expected to start within a week. The recruiter was relentless, bordering on pushy, constantly emphasizing the "urgent need" for someone to fill the role. This should have signaled that the company was in crisis mode, likely due to high employee turnover. But I was flattered and eager, blinded by the initial enthusiasm and the promise of a significant salary increase. Then there was the office itself during my visit. The energy was palpable, but not in a good way. The environment felt sterile, devoid of warmth and camaraderie. Few employees interacted with each other, and there was a palpable sense of tension in the air. The few people I did speak with seemed guarded, providing vague answers to my questions about the company culture and work-life balance. Their hesitation, their reluctance to fully disclose the realities of their work lives, should have sent my Spidey-senses tingling, but instead, I chalked it up to general nervousness and a professional reluctance to overshare. I wish I'd dug deeper, asking more probing questions and insisting on a meeting with someone in a higher-ranking position. What truly sealed the deal, and what I now view as the biggest mistake, was the company's reluctance to provide a detailed job description. The vague outline they gave me contained a long list of responsibilities, which, in retrospect, were far beyond the scope of the initial conversation. This ambiguity, coupled with their insistence that everything would "become clear once I started," should have been a major red flag to my ambitious self. The truth is, I was so eager to prove myself, to climb the corporate ladder, that I ignored all the early warnings. Looking back, it was a lesson learned the hard way. Never be afraid to ask the tough questions, to scrutinize the details, and to trust your instincts. Because sometimes, the fastest offers come with the steepest prices.

Text: Why do women *hate* nerdy men? The notion that women inherently dislike nerdy men is a sweeping generalization that doesn’t hold up under scrutiny. In reality, attraction is multifaceted and deeply personal, shaped by individual preferences, experiences, and societal influences. While some women may gravitate toward confident, extroverted personalities, others find the quiet intellect and passion of nerdy men deeply appealing. The perceived "hate" often stems from misunderstandings or stereotypes rather than any intrinsic quality of nerdiness itself. Nerdy men, like anyone else, possess a wide range of traits—some endearing, others less so. What might be off-putting to some is not their interests or hobbies but behaviors that come across as self-centered, overly intense, or socially unaware. For instance, dominating conversations about niche topics without considering the other person’s interest level can create discomfort. Similarly, a lack of confidence or an inability to read social cues may be misinterpreted as disinterest or awkwardness. It’s worth noting that societal norms play a significant role in shaping these perceptions. Traditional gender roles often emphasize men as assertive and dominant, qualities not always associated with stereotypical nerdiness. However, as societal expectations evolve, so do the qualities women value in partners. Intelligence, creativity, and a genuine passion for learning are increasingly recognized as attractive traits. Many women appreciate the depth and authenticity nerdy men bring to relationships, valuing their ability to engage in meaningful conversations and share unique perspectives. Ultimately, the idea that women universally dislike nerdy men is a myth. Relationships thrive on mutual respect, understanding, and shared values. Nerdy men, like all individuals, have the capacity to foster meaningful connections when they embrace their strengths while remaining mindful of their social interactions. The key lies in finding someone who appreciates them for who they are—quirks and all.  The same principle applies to the notion that women might “*hate*” men who are overly concerned with their physical appearance. The perception of “metrosexuals” or men who prioritize grooming and fashion can often be shaped by preconceived notions and societal expectations. Some might view such behavior as vain or self-absorbed, especially when they assume it comes at the expense of more “masculine” traits. However, like the idea of women “hating” nerdy men, this perception is far more nuanced. Attraction is not a one-size-fits-all equation. What one person finds appealing, another might find off-putting.  There’s a double standard at play here. Women have long been held to impossible beauty standards without much room for error. Now, some men are beginning to pay similar attention to their physical appearance, which isn’t inherently bad. A man who takes care of his health and appearance can be seen as showing self-respect, but only if it isn’t an empty façade.  Ultimately, the issue isn’t so much the interest in grooming itself but the intent behind it. A man who is genuinely focused on self-improvement, both physically and mentally, is likely to be seen in a different light than one solely focused on superficial appearances. Those qualities of confidence and self-awareness, regardless of gender, are almost universally attractive and are far more important as indicators of a deeper character.

Text: Whom did you feel bad for in high school? High school was a veritable petri dish of social dynamics, where allegiances shifted like sand in a desert storm and the most vulnerable often bore the brunt of the prevailing winds. Looking back, I find myself feeling a profound sense of empathy for those who occupied the periphery, the ones who existed in the shadows of the popular crowd, or those who simply never quite found their footing in the relentless social hierarchy. I remember a shy, artistic girl named Sarah, who always carried a sketchbook and seemed to see the world through a different lens. She was kind, intelligent, and fiercely creative, but she struggled to navigate the minefield of teenage social interaction. She was frequently the target of cruel jokes and whispers, and her quiet dignity seemed to make her an even more tempting target for those seeking to exert their dominance. I would often see her alone during lunch breaks, sketching in the corner of the cafeteria, her face a mask of quiet resilience. I never talked to her, a regret that lingers to this day. I was too concerned with my own place in the system, with fitting in, to reach out. Another instance of genuine sorrow involved a kid named Mark, who was relentlessly mocked for his weight and his penchant for collecting comic books. He was an easy target. I don't think I've ever heard so many people, including fellow students, and sometimes even teachers, make fun of someone in their presence. It wasn’t just about the teasing. It was the systematic way in which he was ostracized, excluded from conversations and activities, treated as if he were invisible.  I felt a pang of sympathy for these individuals. I felt they had the raw end of the deal. I felt bad for them for a while. Perhaps it's because I recognized their vulnerability. Or, maybe, I saw a little bit of myself in their struggles, their quiet defiance, their yearning for acceptance. There were the kids who were too different, too awkward, too something to fit into the prescribed molds of high school society. Their pain was palpable, their isolation a heavy mantle. I witnessed firsthand the cruelty that can flourish in the absence of empathy, the casual disregard for the feelings of others, particularly those deemed "other". It was a harsh reality. And it was a potent reminder that high school, for all its supposed significance, is just a temporary phase. The scars of those years, however, could linger long after graduation.

Text: Has your friend ever saved your life? The notion of having one's life saved is a concept that evokes powerful emotions: gratitude, indebtedness, and a profound sense of vulnerability. I've been fortunate to have friends who embody courage and loyalty, but the specific act of having my life saved in a literal, dramatic sense – no, that's not something I can personally claim. However, I have been in situations where the actions of friends undeniably mitigated danger or prevented a far worse outcome. One instance comes to mind. It was a backpacking trip through the rugged terrain. We were pushing ourselves through a particularly challenging trail when I misstepped and lost my footing. For a terrifying moment, I was hurtling towards a steep drop-off. My friend, without hesitation, threw himself forward, grabbing my backpack and pulling me back from the brink. It wasn't a life-or-death scenario in the immediate sense, but the potential consequences of that fall were significant. The resulting injuries could have been debilitating, leaving me stranded miles from civilization. That act of quick thinking and unwavering resolve speaks volumes about the nature of friendship. There was another time, years ago, when I found myself in a precarious situation. It was late one night, walking home from a university event. I was confronted by a group of individuals, their intentions unclear. Tensions were escalating, and the situation felt volatile. Luckily, I was with a close friend who, despite the obvious risk, stepped forward and diffused the situation. His calm demeanor and ability to de-escalate the conflict prevented what could have quickly turned into a physical altercation. His actions, while not necessarily saving my life in the conventional sense, undoubtedly averted a scenario that could have had lasting, negative consequences. Those moments, while not involving a dramatic rescue or a brush with mortality, stand as testaments to the invaluable role friends play in navigating the complexities of life. They are reminders of the bonds we forge, the shared experiences, and the unspoken understanding that binds us together, providing unwavering support when we need it most. It's through these shared experiences, these displays of courage, and the sense of camaraderie, that friendship becomes more than just an association – it transforms into a form of protection.

Text: What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history? The realm of cinema is paved with moments of grandeur, sweeping narratives, and earth-shattering revelations. But, as with life itself, not every crescendo hits the mark. Some movies, despite their build-up, crash and burn at the finish line, leaving audiences with a profound sense of… well, emptiness. To pinpoint the biggest anticlimax in movie history is a subjective pursuit, a matter of individual tastes and expectations. However, several films stand out as prime examples of narrative fizzle, where the promise of something spectacular slowly dissolves into disappointment. A strong contender has always been *War of the Worlds*. Steven Spielberg's adaptation, boasting impressive visuals and a sense of impending doom throughout, culminates in an ending so abrupt and convenient that it undoes much of the tension. How could such a formidable alien threat be vanquished simply due to a common cold? It’s a narrative shortcut that left many viewers feeling cheated. On the other hand, *The Village* offered a different kind of letdown. M. Night Shyamalan, known for his twist endings, crafted a mysterious tale with a sense of foreboding that captivated audiences. The film's trailers hinted at supernatural horrors, creating intense anticipation. The revelation, while unexpected, was more mundane than magical and relied too much on disbelief. The payoff lacked the dramatic weight that had been so meticulously established. Even more contentious is *The Phantom Menace*, which, despite its prequels and the enormous hype, failed to deliver a satisfying conclusion. The climatic space battles, while visually impressive, lacked emotional resonance due to thin character development and convoluted plots. The climactic battle, though visually striking, felt disconnected from the rest of the film, failing to provide a sense of closure. Ultimately, the biggest movie anticlimax is subjective and deeply personal. It hinges on the narrative weight the film tries to build and the ultimate resolution that the film provides. But, what is universally agreed on is that the perfect movie should leave us moved, changed, and fulfilled. And, sometimes, the biggest disappointment is that exact feeling.

Text: As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something? The accusation lodged against me wasn't of malice or neglect, but something arguably more insidious: bias. It wasn't a single, dramatic instance, but a slow build-up of murmurings from students and, eventually, their parents. The whispers started subtly. A comment here about favoring certain students, a question there about the grading system's fairness. At first, I dismissed them as the typical complaints of high school students, or maybe simply misunderstandings. I, after all, considered myself a fair and objective educator, striving to treat all students with equal respect and consideration. I prided myself on fostering an inclusive classroom environment that embraced diversity of thought and background, where everyone could feel comfortable expressing themselves. But the accusations persisted, and I began to feel them like tiny needles pricking at my conscience. The parents, those advocates for students, wanted to believe in my integrity, but their doubts were fueled by perceptions, anecdotes, and perhaps the natural inclination to defend their children. They claimed there was a discernible pattern in my responses to student’s work, a tendency to praise certain viewpoints while subtly, but consistently, devaluing others. My assignments were accused of inadvertently, yet systematically, highlighting specific groups or perspectives while marginalizing others, which made me deeply unsettled. I was not a malicious actor, but the possibility that my own unconscious biases – the product of upbringing, education, and societal pressures – could have influenced my teaching, made me question everything.

Text: What things do people say that make you roll your eyes? The human capacity for verbal absurdity seems limitless, and I find myself frequently rolling my eyes in response to certain utterances. It's not that I'm inherently cynical; rather, it's a matter of encountering the same tired tropes and illogical arguments repeatedly. One of the most common offenders is the blanket statement, the all-encompassing pronouncement that attempts to encapsulate an entire group or phenomenon in a single, facile sentence. "All politicians are corrupt." "Millennials are entitled." "Everyone knows..." The grandiosity of these assertions is matched only by their lack of nuance. They are the intellectual equivalent of fast food—quick to consume but utterly devoid of substance. Another phrase that invariably triggers a visual eye roll is the casual use of hyperbole, the dramatic exaggeration employed to emphasize a point. "I'm *literally* dying of boredom." "This is the *worst* day of my life." While I understand the impulse to express strong emotions, the overuse of extreme language dilutes its impact. It's akin to crying wolf—eventually, nobody believes you. The boy who cried “literally dying of boredom” loses credibility to a degree.  Then there's the victim mentality, the tendency to frame oneself as perpetually wronged without acknowledging personal agency. “I can’t get ahead because…" followed by a series of excuses and external blame. This may be uttered in tandem with a list of misfortunes, implying a predetermined bleak destiny. This type of narrative is a source of frustration as it stifles any constructive engagement and often overlooks the complexities of the situation. Then, the unsolicited advice, particularly when delivered with an air of superiority, is almost guaranteed to initiate a physical response. “You should just…” or if it's "In my experience…" followed by a declaration of assumed superiority, regardless of the topic. However, it’s the ignorance disguised as expertise that truly grinds my gears. The one who speaks with unfounded confidence on subjects they've never rigorously explored. The Dunning-Kruger effect in full force, offering opinions as if they were scientific fact. These people are often unpersuadable, clinging to their misunderstandings with the fervor of true believers. Their pronouncements are like nails on a chalkboard - grating, irritating, and utterly dismissive of reason. These statements are a reminder that, sometimes, silence truly is golden.

Text: At what age did you stop enjoying YA fiction? The transition from youth to adulthood is often marked by a subtle shift in literary tastes. It’s a process as natural as the changing seasons, where the stories that once captivated your imagination begin to feel—well, a bit different. I don’t think there was a specific moment when I abruptly stopped enjoying Young Adult fiction; rather, it was a gradual fading, like the afterglow of a sunset. I recall reading YA novels well into my early twenties, drawn to the familiar themes of self-discovery, first love, and the tumultuous journey toward independence. These stories resonated with the anxieties and aspirations of my own adolescent years.  My fondness for the genre began to wane in tandem with my burgeoning interest in literature of a different stripe. I found myself increasingly drawn to works that explored the complexities of adult life, narratives that delved into the philosophical, socioeconomic, and psychological trenches of the human experience. Authors like Dostoevsky and Camus, with their probing analyses of morality and existence, captured my attention in a way that YA fiction, despite its merits, no longer could. The protagonists and their dilemmas seemed too distilled, too simplified, in comparison to the labyrinthine existences depicted in the novels I had grown to cherish. I began to tire of the formulaic plots, the predictable tropes, and the often-sanitized depictions of reality. The stories felt, in a word, underdeveloped.  That’s not to say I view YA fiction with derision. It remains a valuable genre, one that serves as an entry point to the joys of reading for countless young people. The focus on the inner lives of teenagers and their struggles, the often earnest exploration of life's trials– friendship, romance, betrayal, etc.–remain important components of the human experience. I recognize its continuing relevance, which is not unlike the memory of a cherished childhood toy that has been placed in storage but not forgotten. My appreciation for it has simply matured.

Grant's portrayal is not just entertaining; it's a masterclass in comedic timing and physical humor. His character is ridiculous, yet strangely sympathetic, a testament to the film's genius. The film doesn't shy away from tackling sensitive topics like immigration, loneliness, and the power of community, weaving these themes seamlessly into the narrative. Despite all of these elements, *Paddington 2* goes against all odds and delivers an emotional punch you would never expect. It’s the kind of film that leaves you with a warm, fuzzy feeling, a renewed appreciation for kindness, and a longing to embrace life’s simple joys. The film is a testament to the power of storytelling and the ability of cinema to uplift and inspire. It's a beautiful, charming, and utterly delightful experience, a reminder that even the most improbable tales can become masterpieces. You leave the cinema feeling better than when you walked in.

Text: What is the most obnoxious thing you have seen someone do at the grocery store? Grocery stores are a microcosm of society, a place where humanity's best—and worst—traits often collide. I’ve witnessed a multitude of behaviors over the years, some mundane, others amusing, and a select few that veered into the realm of pure obnoxiousness. The most egregious offender I've ever encountered, without a doubt, was a woman I’ll call *The Coupon Queen*. She wasn’t just a casual coupon user; she was a maestro of discounts, a master of the fine print, and a force of nature when it came to exploiting every possible bargain.  Her reign of terror was confined to the express checkout lane, where she would hold up the line with an arsenal of coupons, each meticulously sorted and categorized. She would demand that the cashier scan and rescan everything, scrutinizing prices with a hawk's eye, and arguing with the poor employee over every cent. I once witnessed her hold up the line for a solid fifteen minutes, all over a loaf of bread that was marked down by a mere twenty-five cents. Her shrill voice cut through the air, her demands echoing across the aisles as she challenged the cashier’s every move. "That's not the right price!" she would shriek, brandishing a crumpled coupon like a weapon. "I have a coupon here for that!"  The rest of us, the onlookers, were held hostage by her antics. We shifted from foot to foot, grumbling under our breath, our carts overflowing as we waited. The cashier, bless her heart, maintained a semblance of composure, trying to appease *The Coupon Queen* while the line grew longer and longer. The tension mounted as the minutes ticked by, the air thick with frustration and the scent of discounted produce. What was most baffling was the sheer volume of coupons. She had coupons for everything imaginable – for cereal, for toilet paper, even for individual pieces of fruit. It’s as if she had dedicated her life to finding the most obscure ways to save a few pennies. Finally, after what felt like an eternity, she triumphantly completed her transaction, a mountain of groceries secured at a fraction of their original cost. She then proceeded to give the cashier a lecture on time management, before strutting off with a triumphant grin, leaving a trail of disgruntled shoppers in her wake. It was a display of selfishness and entitlement that etched itself into my memory, a stark reminder that even the most mundane errands can reveal the depths of human obnoxiousness. I often wonder if she ever realized the chaos she created, or if she simply reveled in her perceived victory. Either way, *The Coupon Queen* remains a cautionary tale – a testament to the power of a well-timed coupon, and the utter lack of consideration for others.

Text: If all animals were horse-sized, which would be the most majestic to ride into battle? The battlefield, a canvas of chaos, would be a stage for awe-inspiring spectacles if animals were scaled to the size of horses. While the romantic notion of riding a majestic lion or a fiercely loyal wolf into the fray might stir the soul, practicality dictates a different champion. Considering factors like temperament, physical prowess, and overall suitability for warfare, the most regal steed would have to be the elephant.  Imagine the panorama of war, an army of horse-sized creatures surging forward. The elephant, with its colossal presence, would become an unassailable fortress amidst the carnage. Its thick hide would offer protection against arrows and other projectiles. Its massive frame would effortlessly crush any foe daring to stand in its path. The sheer momentum of such a beast, charging at full tilt, would be enough to shatter enemy lines and scatter the opposition.  The elephant’s intelligence and social nature are essential factors. Unlike a lone predator, such as a giant tiger or a bear, elephants are known for their complex social structures and their ability to cooperate. A herd of elephant-sized elephants could function as a cohesive unit, implementing battle strategies and supporting one another. The bond between rider and beast would be all the more crucial, of course.  Furthermore, the elephant, historically revered as a symbol of strength and power, carries an inherent sense of nobility. Whether it is the elephant’s tusks, or the way it majestically moves onward, riding one into battle would send a message to opponents: they are to contend with a force of supreme power. In the chaos of a battlefield, such a creature would create an aura of invincibility, giving the rider the edge, and providing the assurance that only few can muster. Its trunk, capable of grasping and manipulating objects, could serve as a formidable weapon itself, and the ears would become giant sails, adding to their intimidation, and in full attack mode, the elephant is a true weapon of warfare the likes of which had, and will likely never exist again.

Text: What is the lamest “benefit” you’ve been offered by an employer? Ah, the "perks" of the job. The siren song of corporate culture, designed to lure you in and keep you tethered to your desk. Over the years, I’ve encountered a fair share of these supposed incentives, each more underwhelming than the last. But one stands out as particularly egregious, a testament to the disconnect between employer expectations and employee desires: the "wellness program" that offered a discount on… *cough*... cigarettes. Yes, you read that right.  It was a mid-sized advertising agency, renowned–or perhaps infamous–for its long hours, high-stress environment, and a culture that seemed to actively encourage unhealthy habits. The "wellness program" was touted as a way to promote employee well-being, but its primary offering was a meager reduction on the price of tobacco products. The irony was thick enough to choke on, and the cynicism palpable. Here they were, ostensibly concerned about our health, while simultaneously incentivizing a habit known to actively erode it. This program felt less like genuine care and more like a band-aid slapped clumsily over a festering wound. It was a clear indicator that the company’s priorities lay elsewhere, and that employee well-being was a mere afterthought. It was a blatant disregard for the health of its employees. This was not only a lame benefit, it was an insult. It was a symbol, writ large, of everything that was wrong with that company, and a reminder that sometimes, the gap between intention and execution is vast. What's worse, it was a signal to the employees that they weren't valued, a sentiment that reverberated throughout the workplace. You were at your wits end. The whole situation made you question your sanity. It was simply ridiculous.

Text: Can you provide some examples of average actors delivering great performances due to well-written characters? The convergence of a compelling narrative and an actor’s inherent skill can often birth cinematic magic. The annals of film history are replete with examples of performers, not necessarily considered A-listers, transcending their usual range to deliver truly memorable performances thanks to the strength of their character. Take, for instance, the case of Heath Ledger in *The Dark Knight*. While Ledger’s pre-Joker roles showcased talent, it was Christopher Nolan’s nuanced writing of The Joker that allowed Ledger to explode onto the scene, crafting a portrayal that redefined villainy. The character’s inherent chaos, unpredictability, and philosophical underpinnings provided a rich canvas for Ledger to paint a performance that earned him a posthumous Oscar. Then there’s Christoph Waltz in *Inglourious Basterds*. Waltz, prior to this role, wasn't a household name. Quentin Tarantino’s writing of the eloquent, chilling, and yet utterly charming Colonel Hans Landa gave Waltz the spotlight. The character’s layered complexities—his charm, his intelligence, and his ruthlessness—allowed Waltz to mesmerize audiences, making him an overnight sensation. Similarly, look at Kathy Bates in *Misery*. Her portrayal of Annie Wilkes, a disturbed fan, is terrifying not strictly because of Bates’ acting prowess, but due to Stephen King’s masterful creation of a character teetering on the edge of sanity. Wilkes is both vulnerable and menacing, a duality that Bates leverages to deliver a performance that is as disturbing as it is captivating. One cannot also overlook the impact of Anthony Hopkins’ portrayal of Hannibal Lecter in *The Silence of the Lambs*. While Hopkins had a distinguished career before, it was the well-crafted Lecter, with his refined intellect, sharp wit, and underlying savagery, who catapulted him into the stratosphere. The dialogue, the subtle gestures, the calculated mannerisms—all these elements, carefully woven into Thomas Harris’ narrative, allowed Hopkins to create a character that has haunted viewers for decades. These examples highlight a crucial truth: a well-written character allows an actor to shine, often exceeding expectations. The script, in these instances, became the launchpad, enabling these actors' talents to ascend to unprecedented heights.

It remains a testament to the fact that the universe loves a good surprise, a fleeting moment of the absurd that defies all logical explanation. Text: What's the most ridiculous thing a coworker told on you to your boss for? Ah, the labyrinthine complexities of workplace dynamics! It's a realm where ambition, camaraderie, and, occasionally, petty grievances collide. I've witnessed my share of office antics, but one particular incident stands out as a monument to the absurd. It involved a coworker I'll refer to as Janice, a woman whose talent for drama was matched only by her flair for exaggeration. The story started innocently enough: a company-wide potluck. As these events often do, it became a microcosm of our office. There was the usual assortment of culinary triumphs and, shall we say, less successful attempts. I had brought a rather elaborate mango salsa, a recipe I had perfected over years of experimentation with Trinidadian peppers and sun-ripened fruit. Apparently, this simple act of communal sharing was enough to ignite Janice's ire. The next morning, I was summoned to my boss’s office. I walked in with a knot of confusion in my stomach, wondering what transgression I had committed. The answer? My mango salsa was “a blatant attempt to undermine her culinary contributions.” According to Janice, my vibrant condiment had “stolen the spotlight” from her bland, store-bought potato salad. The details, as relayed by my boss, were both outrageous and hilarious. Janice claimed my salsa’s color palette was “offensive” to her sensibilities. She accused me of using “exotic flavors” to make everyone forget her “traditional” dish. Apparently, the fact that the mango salsa was, in fact, enjoyed by the majority of the party-goers, was further proof of my malicious intent. The entire narrative was so preposterous that I barely knew how to respond. I tried to explain that I was simply trying to share a dish that I was proud of. Then I recalled how Janice didn’t bring anything to the event until it was almost over. My explanation, however, seemed to fall on deaf ears. The boss—bless his heart—tried to mediate, offering platitudes about teamwork and avoiding office drama. Ultimately, nothing happened, except that Janice continued to give me the side-eye and I became forevermore mindful of the power of a well-prepared mango salsa. The whole episode was a comical reminder that, in the workplace, the most absurd accusations can be launched for the flimsiest of reasons. Never underestimate the power of jealousy, especially when combined with a dash of potato salad and a whole lot of imagination.
